01Chapter 1 · Introduction

Introduction — Evals kyun zaroori hain

Pichhle kuch saalon me large language models (LLMs) itni tezi se aage badhe hain ki organizations unhe har jagah embed kar rahi hain — customer service, content creation, decision support, information extraction, aur bhi bahut kuch. In software products ko LLM applications kehte hain, aur unke andar jo LLM-driven component decisions leta hai, tools call karta hai aur output banata hai, use LLM agent kehte hain. Lekin adoption us speed se badh raha hai, jis speed se hum in systems ko systematically evaluate kar paate hain — aur ye gap hi is book ki kahani hai.

Bina evaluation ke ship karne ki keemat

Ek unevaluated agent ship karne ke consequences serious ho sakte hain. Late 2022 ki ek mashhoor kahani hai: ek passenger ne apni grandmother ke nidhan ke baad last-minute flight book karne ke liye ek airline ki website par customer support chatbot se poocha ki kya use bereavement fare (funeral ya death ke liye travel par milne wala discounted ticket) mil sakta hai. Chatbot ne galat jawab diya — usne kaha ki regular fare book karo aur 90 din ke andar bereavement discount refund ke roop me claim kar lo. Airline ki asal policy thi ki bereavement discount sirf flight se pehle request kiya ja sakta tha, baad me nahi. Jab passenger ne refund apply kiya to airline ne mana kar diya. Mamla tribunal tak gaya, aur February 2024 me faisla passenger ke favour me aaya. Tribunal ne airline ka ye argument reject kar diya ki chatbot ek "separate legal entity" hai — airline ko hallucinated policy ke liye liable mana gaya, damages pay karne pade, aur chatbot ko website se hata diya gaya.

Kisi ko exactly nahi pata ki chatbot ne galat jawab kyun diya. Ho sakta hai use policy text par train ya prompt kiya gaya ho jise usne galat tareeke se paraphrase kar diya ho. Ho sakta hai usne dusri airlines ki policies ki language utha li ho, jahan retroactive bereavement claims allowed hote hain. Jo baat pakki hai woh ye hai ki kisi ne ye failure pakdi hi nahi, jab tak ek customer ne us par bharosa nahi kar liya. Common policy questions par chatbot ke jawabon ki systematic check is discrepancy ko launch se pehle hi flag kar sakti thi. Aise cases dikhate hain ki evaluation kyun zaroori hai: production me galat jawab dene wale agents serious legal aur reputational cost la sakte hain.

Evaluation launch par khatm nahi hoti

Evaluation sirf launch se pehle ki cheez nahi hai. Prelaunch evaluation system ko users ke saamne aane se pehle test karta hai; production monitoring system ko live hone ke baad continuously check karta hai. Dono evaluation process ka hissa hain, lekin dono alag problems pakadte hain. Prelaunch evaluation failures ko users tak pahunchne se pehle dhoondhta hai, jabki production monitoring un failures ko pakadta hai jo sirf real world me dikhte hain — jahan input distributions shift hoti hain aur user behavior unpredictable hota hai. Production monitoring Chapter 9 me detail me aata hai.

LLM applications traditional software se alag kyun hain

Traditional software ke opposite, LLM applications consistent, repeatable responses nahi dete, aur unke paas koi formal specification nahi hoti ki unhe kya logic karna chahiye aur kya nahi. Wahi input alag runs me alag outputs de sakta hai, aur outputs aise tareekon se galat ho sakte hain jinka andaza lagana mushkil hai. Kabhi-kabhi, jaise airline wali kahani me, woh obviously galat hote hain. Dusri baar issue describe karna hi mushkil hota hai. Ek output factually sahi ho sakta hai lekin inappropriate ho sakta hai — "vibes off" lag sakte hain — ya convincing sound karte hue poori tarah galat ho sakta hai. Ye ambiguities evaluation ko conventional software testing se, aur traditional machine learning (ML) se bhi, fundamentally alag bana deti hain. Traditional ML me outputs well-defined hote hain — numbers, classes, ya structured predictions — aur aksar ground truth labels hote hain, jin par accuracy ya F1 score jaise standard metrics lagte hain. LLM output open-ended, unstructured aur aksar subjective hota hai.

Agent vs application — farq kyun matter karta hai

Book me "agent" shabd broadly use hota hai. Iska range ek single LLM call bina tools ke (sabse simple case) se lekar ek aise system tak hai jo loop me chalta hai, kai tools call karta hai aur har request par kai decisions leta hai. Chapter 2 is range ko concrete examples ke saath samjhata hai. Agent aur application ke beech ka distinction evaluation ke liye useful hai. Agent woh LLM-driven component hai jo reason karta hai, tools call karta hai aur output banata hai. Application uske aas-paas ki har cheez hai: user interface, database, API layer, deployment infrastructure. Kuch failures agent se aati hain (jaise galat tool call, galat reasoning, galat output format). Dusri application ke aas-paas se aati hain (jaise toota hua user interface, missing data, slow response time). Ye book agent-level evaluation par focus karti hai.

Evaluation ka core challenge

Evaluation ka core challenge ye hai: hum kaise assess karein ki ek LLM agent adequately perform kar raha hai ya nahi, aur kaise diagnose karein ki woh kahan fail ho raha hai? Ye book in sawalon ka practical foundation banati hai, aise methods ke saath jo aap apne projects par apply kar sakte hain. Aage ke chapters me aap seekhenge ki evaluation ka matlab kya hai, Three Gulfs framework se failures kahan hote hain, aur Analyze-Measure-Improve lifecycle jo poori book ko structure deta hai.

Yaad rakho: Adoption evaluation se tezi se badh raha hai. Ek systematic check launch se pehle — jaise chatbot ke policy jawabon ko common questions par test karna — ek costly public failure ko rok sakta hai. Evaluation ek baar ka check nahi, poori lifecycle ka saathi hai.
SOURCESource: Evals for AI Engineers, O'Reilly, Chapter 1 — Introduction

01.1Chapter 1 · Introduction

What Is Evaluation? — LLM apps me evaluation ka matlab

Evaluation ek LLM application me quality ko samajhne aur measure karne ka systematic process hai. Isme failure patterns ka qualitative analysis bhi aata hai aur unki frequency ka quantitative measurement bhi. Ek achhi evaluation aise results deti hai jo interpretable aur actionable hon — matlab aap samajh sakein ki kya galat hai aur use fix karne ke liye kya karna hai.

Metric hamesha ek number nahi hota

Kuch cases me evaluation ek quantitative metric deti hai. Example ke liye, agar aap travel planning assistant bana rahe hain, to aap measure kar sakte hain ki system kitni baar budget ke andar valid flight aur hotel options deta hai, ya itineraries user ki constraints satisfy karte hain ya nahi. Dusre cases me "metric" zyada judgment ke saath banta hai. Experts ka ek set, ya kabhi-kabhi product team khud, outputs ko review karke clarity, tone ya usefulness jaise qualities par rate karti hai. Dono approaches rigor ke ek spectrum par aate hain: quick, informal checks jo early iteration ko guide karte hain, se lekar carefully defined rubrics aur systematic sampling tak jo production systems ko support karte hain.

Ek application, kai evaluations

Ek single application ko usually multiple evaluations chahiye hoti hain, har ek performance ki ek alag dimension capture karne ke liye design ki gayi. Ek hi evaluation se sab kuch cover nahi hota — factual accuracy, tone, format, completeness, safety — har dimension ke liye alag check chahiye. Evaluations ko application me kai tareekon se integrate kiya ja sakta hai:

  • Monitoring: background me continuously chalne wale checks, jo drift ya degradation ko time ke saath detect karte hain.
  • Guardrails: critical path me lagi hui evaluations, jo system ko allow karti hain ki outputs predefined criteria fail karein to block kare, retry kare, ya fallback par jaye.
  • Improvement mechanisms: evaluations jo feedback generate karti hain — jaise model ko aur train karne ke liye labeled examples, prompt me directly include kiye jaane wale curated example inputs aur outputs (jinhe few-shot examples kehte hain), ya failure cases ki systematic identification jo architectural changes ko motivate karti hai.
  • Model migration: evaluations jo aapko alag model versions ki performance compare karne deti hain, aur informed decisions lene me madad karti hain ki kab naye model par migrate karna hai.

Hum evaluations par bharosa karte hain errors detect karne ke liye, user trust maintain karne ke liye, safety constraints enforce karne ke liye, ongoing behavior monitor karne ke liye, aur systematic improvement guide karne ke liye. Matlab evaluation sirf ek test nahi hai — woh product ke health ka ek ongoing system hai.

Evaluation kya nahi hai

Evaluation ko sirf "accuracy score" samajhna galti hai. Ek travel assistant 90% baar sahi flights de sakta hai lekin 10% baar budget violate kar sakta hai — aur wahi 10% users ka trust tod deta hai. Isliye evaluation ka kaam hai quality ko samajhna — kya fail ho raha hai, kitni baar ho raha hai, aur kyun ho raha hai — sirf ek number report karna nahi. Qualitative reading (traces padhna, failure patterns samajhna) aur quantitative measurement (frequency ginna) dono saath chalte hain, aur ek ke bina dusra adhoora hai.

Yaad rakho: Ek achhi evaluation interpretable aur actionable hoti hai. Agar result dekh kar aapko ye samajh na aaye ki kya fix karna hai, to evaluation abhi adhoori hai — chahe number kitna bhi impressive kyun na lage.

01.2Chapter 1 · Introduction

Evaluation Throughout the Lifecycle

Evaluation LLM lifecycle ke har stage par dikhti hai. Har stage par — pretraining, post-training, aur phir unke upar bane applications — evaluation ka role alag hota hai, kyunki har stage ke goals aur constraints alag hote hain. In stages ko samajhna ye clarify karta hai ki kaunsi capabilities test ho rahi hain, aur kyun koi single evaluation framework har jagah apply nahi ho sakta.

Pretraining — foundation model banana

Pretraining lifecycle ka pehla stage hai, jahan ek foundation model scratch se banta hai. Ek bada neural network massive text (aur kabhi-kabhi code) collections par ek hi objective ke saath expose hota hai: sequence me next token predict karna. Token text ki sabse chhoti unit hai jo model ek baar me padhta ya likhta hai — usually characters ki ek chhoti sequence, lagbhag ek word ya word ke hisse ke barabar. Example: sentence "The chatbot answered the question" tokens me toot sakta hai — The, chat, bot, answered, the, question. Models ek baar me ek token padhte aur generate karte hain, aur ek API call ki cost usually tokens in aur out ki sankhya me measure hoti hai. Pretraining ke dauraan, billions of examples par next-token prediction karke model broad linguistic knowledge aur kuch reasoning aur world knowledge ki capacity seekhta hai.

Pretraining bade research labs aur commercial model providers karte hain. Is process ke liye substantial computational resources chahiye hote hain, aksar hundreds of millions of dollars ki cost. Is stage par evaluation intrinsic hoti hai — matlab hum measure karte hain ki model unseen text par next token sahi predict karta hai ya nahi. Ek common metric hai perplexity, held-out text par per-token average negative log-likelihood. Kam perplexity ka matlab hai model unseen data se kam "surprised" hai. Pretraining evaluation me scaling-law analysis bhi aati hai, jo track karti hai ki compute aur training data badhne par loss kaise kam hota hai. Ye metrics batate hain ki model ne language ke statistical patterns absorb kiye hain ya nahi, lekin ye nahi batate ki model un downstream tasks ke liye useful hai ya nahi jo log asal me LLMs ke saath banate hain.

Post-training — model ko practical use ke liye adapt karna

Post-training ek pretrained model ko lekar use practical use ke liye adapt karta hai. Sirf next-token prediction par train hue models bhi kai unseen tasks par generalize kar lete hain — tasks jin par LLMs ko explicitly pretrain nahi kiya gaya tha. Post-training is ability par build karke model ko un behaviors ki taraf steer karta hai jin ki users ko parwah hai, jaise instructions follow karna, topic par rehna, aur unsafe responses se bachna.

Post-training ke usually do parts hote hain. Pehle, model provider model ko prompts ke curated examples aur achhe responses par fine-tune karta hai, taaki model woh format seekh le jo log chahte hain. Dusre, provider preference data use karta hai — response ke pairs jin me ek human ne chuna ki kaunsa behtar hai — taaki model ko preferred style ki taraf aur nudge kiya ja sake. Recent post-training methods me direct preference optimization (DPO) aur process reward models aate hain, jo model ke internal reasoning ko badalte hain. Kuch models reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) bhi use karte hain taaki long chains of thought ko step-by-step reasoning ke saath train kiya ja sake. Post-training method is baat ko affect karta hai ki application me model kis tarah ki errors karta hai; isliye ye jaanna useful hai ki kaunsa method use hua tha, chahe aap training khud na chala rahe hon.

Ye book in techniques ko detail me cover nahi karti, kyunki zyadaatar engineers model se in steps ke baad interact karte hain. Is stage par evaluation raw next-token accuracy measure karne se shift hokar model ko aise benchmarks par chalane par aa jati hai jo user-facing tasks ko approximate karte hain — question-answering, reasoning challenges, safety aur bias tests, aur coding. Ye evaluations model providers khud design aur run karte hain, aur unke results aksar headline benchmarks ke roop me report hote hain.

Application stage — jahan zyadaatar engineers kaam karte hain

Application stage woh hai jahan zyadaatar engineers aur product managers LLMs se engage karte hain. Is point par model pehle se train aur align ho chuka hota hai, aur kaam hai use ek concrete workflow me integrate karna — jaise emails triage karna, customer support me madad karna, ya documents analyze karna. Is stage par evaluation ko specific application ke goals aur data ke hisaab se tailor karna padta hai. Kuch cases me existing post-training evaluations task se directly overlap karti hain. Example: ek coding assistant established programming benchmarks par bharosa kar sakta hai. Zyadaatar cases me, lekin, application public leaderboards me represent hi nahi hoti. Contracts review karne wala system, medical notes summarize karne wala system, ya compliance check karne wala system — in sab ko apne evaluation methods chahiye honge.

Isliye responsibility application development team par aati hai: success ka matlab define karna, appropriate metrics design karna, aur monitoring implement karna taaki verify ho sake ki system apne intended use ke liye reliably behave karta hai.

Applications me evaluation — teen mushkilein

Application stage par model pehle se train ho chuka hota hai. Kaam uske aas-paas build karne ka hai. Aapko decide karna hota hai ki product ko kya achieve karna chahiye, us goal ko prompts aur agent logic me translate karna hota hai, aur phir verify karna hota hai ki model ke outputs acceptable hain. In steps me se har ek apni mushkilein laata hai:

  • Objectives pehle vague hote hain: "summarize emails" jaisa goal simple lagta hai, lekin ambiguities tab dikhti hain jab aap outputs inspect karte hain — kitna detailed, kis format me, aur kya exclude karna hai?
  • Instructions me gaps ho sakte hain: natural language me likhe gaye prompts aur agent logic rarely poora intent capture karte hain, jisse inconsistent ya incomplete behavior hota hai.
  • Behavior naye data par badal jata hai: ek setup jo handful test cases par kaam karta hai, real inputs ki variability se milte hi fail ho sakta hai.

Practically, ye issues LLM applications banate waqt baar-baar dikhte hain. In challenges ke baare me zyada systematically sochne ke liye book Three Gulfs framework use karti hai, jo teen jagah naam deta hai jahan development tootne lagti hai — comprehension, specification aur generalization. Har gulf ek alag point highlight karta hai jahan development typically galat hoti hai, aur har ek ko address karne ke liye alag strategy chahiye — ek theme jo poori book me wapas aati rahegi.

Yaad rakho: Pretraining me evaluation poochhti hai "kya model language seekh gaya?", post-training me "kya model useful tasks kar sakta hai?", aur application stage me "kya system mere users ke liye sahi behave karta hai?" — teeno ke jawab alag tareekon se milte hain, aur teeno ke liye alag evaluation chahiye.

01.3Chapter 1 · Introduction

Three Gulfs — Comprehension, Execution, Evaluation

LLM applications banane ki challenges ko samajhne ka ek useful tareeka hai Three Gulfs model. Ye model teen common gaps highlight karta hai jinka developers ko saamna hota hai jab woh applications banate aur evaluate karte hain. In gaps ko kehte hain — comprehension, specification, aur generalization. Poori book me is framework ko use kiya jata hai ye diagnose karne ke liye ki application kyun fail ho rahi hai, aur use fix karne ki sabse appropriate strategy kaunsi hai.

Ek example: email processing agent

Ek agent ko imagine karo jo organization ko aane wale emails process karta hai. Goal hai sender ka naam extract karna, key requests summarize karna, aur email categorize karna. Pehli nazar me ye straightforward lagta hai. Lekin development ka har stage Three Gulfs me alag challenges expose karta hai.

Gulf of Comprehension — developer aur data ke beech

Pehla gulf developer aur data ke beech hai. Effective prompts aur agents banane ke liye aapko solid grasp chahiye ki aapke inputs asal me kaise dikhte hain. Uske bina aap task ke imagined version ke against design karenge, real wale ke against nahi. Email example me, agar aap prompt draft karte waqt sirf handful clean, well-written emails dekhte hain, to aapki instructions un cases par fine kaam karengi. Lekin production data me forwards, long quoted threads wale replies, multiple languages me signatures, aur PDFs se copy kiya gaya poorly formatted text bhi hoga. Ek prompt jo in realities ko ignore karta hai, LLM ko lead kar sakta hai — jaise naye message ke bajaye poori quoted thread summarize kar dena, ya signature block ko main request samajh lena.

Gulf of Comprehension sirf inputs par nahi, outputs par bhi apply hota hai. Hume ye bhi clear sense chahiye ki LLM un inputs par kaise behave karta hai. Aap har output nahi padh sakte, lekin phir bhi aapko common tareeke pehchanne hain jin me woh succeed karta hai aur jin me fail hota hai. Warna kuch achhe examples se mislead hokar aap un patterns ko miss kar denge jo sirf scale par dikhte hain. Email agent me, LLM usually sender extract karke decent summary likh sakta hai. Lekin jab aap closely dekhte hain, to recurring mistakes dikh sakti hain — LLM kai naam mention hone par galat naam utha sakta hai, lambi messages me key details drop kar sakta hai, ya confidentiality notices jaisi boilerplate ko summary me copy kar sakta hai. Ye failures kabhi-kabhi hi hote hain, lekin agar hote hain to system users ko unreliable lagega. Gulf of Comprehension ko bridge karne ka matlab hai aise strategies develop karna jo aapke inputs aur outputs dono ko scale par characterize karein, taaki aap jaan sakein ki data asal me kaisa dikhta hai aur system asal me kaise behave karta hai, bina sab kuch haath se inspect kiye.

Gulf of Specification — developer aur LLM agent ke beech

Dusra gulf hai jo hum chahte hain aur jo hum asal me LLM ko batate hain, uske beech. Hamara intent (jo task humare dimaag me hai) aksar sirf loosely capture hota hai un prompts ya agent logic me jo hum likhte hain. Natural language imprecise hoti hai, aur phrasing me chhote gaps behavior me bade differences la sakte hain. Instruction lo: "Extract the sender's name and summarize the key requests in this email." Pehli nazar me ye specific lagta hai, lekin important details unstated reh jati hain. Summary paragraph honi chahiye ya bulleted list? Sender display name hona chahiye, poora email address, ya dono? Implicit requests include karne hain ya sirf explicit ones? Summary kitna concise hona chahiye?

LLM ye choices aapke liye fill nahi kar sakta. Agar aap unhe explicit nahi banate, to system guess karega, aur woh guesses hamesha aapki expectations se match nahi karenge. Isi liye same agent ke do runs alag formats me outputs de sakte hain, varying levels of detail ke saath, ya edge cases ko inconsistent tareeke se handle kar sakte hain. Gulf of Specification yehi gap hai — hamare intent aur hamari instructions ke beech. Ise close karne ke liye expectations ko explicit banana padta hai aur unhe us data ke saath closely align karna padta hai jo agent asal me dekhega.

Gulf of Generalization — data aur LLM agent ke beech

Teesra gulf hai data jo aapka system dekhta hai aur LLM us par kaise generalize karta hai, uske beech. Chahe aapko apne inputs ki solid grasp ho aur aapne clear, well-scoped prompt likha ho, phir bhi LLM errors karega. LLMs perfect nahi hote, aur woh mistakes karenge. Imagine karo aapne clearly specify kiya hai ki system ko sender ka naam email header se extract karna chahiye. Zyadaatar baar LLM instruction follow karta hai. Lekin kabhi-kabhi, jab email ki body me kisi aur vyakti ka naam aata hai (jaise ek public figure), to LLM galat naam return kar deta hai. Aapki data ki samajh ya aapke prompt me kuch galat nahi tha. LLM ne instructions ko consistently apply karne me fail kiya. Ho sakta hai LLM apne training data me dekhe gaye naamon ke favour me zyada biased ho. Yehi Gulf of Generalization hai: ye fact ki LLMs unpredictably behave kar sakte hain, chahe comprehension aur specification achhe se handle ho. Ye errors usually tabhi visible hote hain jab system real-world data ki poori variety se milta hai. Aur ye unavoidable hain: models kitne bhi advanced ho jayein, hamesha cases honge jahan woh galat output denge.

Teeno gulfs dusre domains me bhi

Three Gulfs sirf email processing tak limited nahi hain. Ek customer support chatbot me, Gulf of Comprehension customer queries ki poori variety ke baare me hai — multilingual messages, typos aur multi-part questions. Gulf of Specification "achha" response kaisa dikhta hai ye define karne ke baare me hai; ek bot jo escalate karne ke bajaye apologize karta hai, woh galat instructions follow kar raha hai, aur explicit rules ke bina bot guess karega. Gulf of Generalization tab dikhta hai jab bot billing questions achhe se handle karta hai lekin product-specific questions par fail ho jata hai, jin ke use kam examples dekhe hain. Ek code generation assistant me, Gulf of Comprehension is baare me hai ki developers asal me kya describe karte hain — aksar vague requests, incomplete context aur undocumented internal APIs ke references. Gulf of Specification output format, error handling aur style conventions define karne ke baare me hai. Gulf of Generalization tab dikhta hai jab model sahi Python generate karta hai lekin kam common languages ya complex multi-file changes par fail ho jata hai. Har application ki evaluation strategy is par depend karti hai ki failure ka primary source kaunsa gulf hai.

LLM agent evaluation challenging kyun hai

LLM applications evaluate karna challenging hai kyunki har application ko teeno gulfs ko apne context me phir se bridge karna padta hai. Evaluation ek baar ka check nahi hai. Ye ek iterative process hai jahan requirements tabhi clear hoti hain jab aap real outputs ke saath interact karte hain. Jab aap outputs examine karna shuru karte hain (Gulf of Comprehension close karte hue), to aapko inevitably mistakes milengi. Agla sawaal ye hai ki kya ye mistakes incomplete specification ki wajah se hain ya generalization ki failures ki wajah se. Agar prompt requirement ko explicit nahi banata, to aap use behtar instructions ya agent design se fix kar sakte hain. Agar prompt pehle se well-specified hai aur LLM phir bhi fail karta hai, to issue generalization me hai, aur automated evaluations measure karne me madad kar sakti hain ki woh failure kitni baar hota hai.

Applications is me bhi alag hoti hain ki users par kitna bharosa kiya ja sakta hai ki woh gulfs ko khud bridge kar lein. Ek coding assistant me, hum assume kar sakte hain ki programmers ki agency high hai. Woh requirements precisely specify karna jante hain, generated code padh aur debug kar sakte hain (comprehension), aur tests chala sakte hain jo expose karte hain ki LLM generalize karne me kab fail hua. Iske contrast me, ek LLM-powered personal stylist ko lo. Outfit maangne wala user shayad requirements clearly specify karna na janta ho. Application ko khud clarifying questions poochne pad sakte hain — jaise weather ya formality ke baare me — taaki specification gaps kam hon. Users generalization failures ko aasani se detect bhi nahi kar sakte: agar LLM casual winter wear ke liye achhe suggestions deta hai, to woh assume kar sakte hain ki woh winter weddings ke liye bhi achha perform karega — ek assumption jo sahi na bhi ho. Effective evaluation ke liye har application me har gulf ke stakes ke baare me sochna padta hai. Jahan stakes zyada hain — kyunki users mistakes khud aasani se catch nahi kar sakte ya errors ki cost significant hai — wahan gaps close karne ke liye zyada rigorous processes design karne padenge. Three Gulfs framework teams ko failures discuss karne ke liye ek shared vocabulary deta hai: debugging ke waqt aap jaldi identify kar sakte hain ki problem "specification failure" hai ya "generalization failure", aur sahi fix chun sakte hain, bajaye iske ki vague tareeke se debate karein ki model "kaam nahi kar raha".

Analyze-Measure-Improve lifecycle — gulfs ko bridge karna

Three Gulfs batate hain ki LLM applications kahan galat hoti hain. Is book me evaluation ko Analyze-Measure-Improve lifecycle ke through approach kiya jata hai. Ye iterative framework evaluation ka use karke gulfs ko bridge karta hai — failures ko systematically samajhna (Analyze), unhe quantify karna (Measure), aur unhe fix karna (Improve).

  • Analyze: Cycle Analyze se shuru hota hai. Is stage par aap real inputs aur outputs dekhte hain taaki samajh sakein ki system asal me kaise behave karta hai. Goal failure modes identify karna hai, abhi unhe quantify karna nahi. Analyze sabse directly Gulf of Comprehension se judta hai, lekin ye specification gaps aur generalization issues bhi surface karta hai — aap aksar teeno tarah ki problems ek hi trace-reading session me discover karte hain. Practically, iska matlab hai traces padhna (har request par agent ne kya kiya, uska poora record), users ya domain experts se baat karna ki "correct" kaisa dikhta hai, aur system ke fail hone ke tareekon ki list banana. Chapter 3 isko detail me cover karta hai. Imagine karo aap email summaries ka ek batch review karte hain aur do recurring problems notice karte hain: LLM kabhi signatures se irrelevant text include kar leta hai, aur kabhi sabse important request omit kar deta hai. Ye observations batati hain ki cheezein kahan toot-ti hain aur clues deti hain ki issue poor specification hai ya generalization failure.
  • Measure: Analyze ke baad aapko pata hota hai ki system kis tarah ki mistakes karta hai. Kuch clearly specification problems hongi: prompt ne kaafi nahi kaha, to fix obvious hai. Dusri generalization errors lagengi: prompt clear tha, lekin LLM phir bhi misbehave karta hai. Measure step in generalization issues ko quantify karne ke baare me hai. Key sawaal hai: har failure mode asal me kitni baar hota hai, aur kya rate itna kam hai ki system usable hai? Measurement ke bina aap handful traces ke impressions par bharosa kar rahe hain, jo dono direction me misleading ho sakte hain — kuch bure examples ek achhe system ko toota hua dikha sakte hain, aur kuch achhe examples ek toote hue system ko achha dikha sakte hain. Scale par measure karne ke liye aap evaluators design karte hain (automated checks) jo traces ko human review ke bina score kar sakte hain. Ye code-based rules ho sakte hain, ya ek aur LLM judge ke roop me use ho sakta hai (Chapter 5 me cover hota hai). Imagine karo aapka LLM prompt clarify karne ke baad bhi kabhi signature blocks ko summaries me kheench leta hai. Aap ek rule-based check banate hain jo thousands of outputs me boilerplate phrases flag karta hai aur paate hain ki ye 8% cases me hota hai. Measurement batata hai ki failure occasional annoyance hai ya systematic problem.
  • Improve: Aakhri step Improve hai: Analyze aur Measure ne jo uncover kiya hai, uske basis par system ko adjust karne ka faisla. Jo path aap follow karte hain, woh errors ke source par depend karta hai. Agar woh specification gaps se aate hain, to fix usually prompt ko tighten karna ya agent logic adjust karna hai. Agar woh generalization failures se aate hain, to stronger interventions chahiye ho sakte hain, jaise zyada examples add karna, retrieval refine karna, ya labeled data par fine-tuning karna. Chapter 12 in improvement strategies ko detail me cover karta hai, effort level ke hisaab se organize karke — quick prompt edits se lekar model-level changes tak. Imagine karo measurements dikhate hain ki key requests miss hona isliye hota hai kyunki prompt ne detail ka level kabhi specify hi nahi kiya. Ye specification fix hai: aap instruction revise karte hain — "Summarize the sender's requests in three concise bullet points." Lekin naam confusion ka issue clear prompt ke baad bhi bana rehta hai. Woh generalization problem hai, aur use fix karne ke liye labeled training data add karna pad sakta hai, ya application ko redesign karna pad sakta hai taaki sender ko email metadata se extract kiya jaye, bajaye iske ki LLM par bharosa kiya jaye ki woh body parse karega.

Har pass is cycle se aapko apne gulfs ko samajhne me madad milti hai aur aap apne application ke liye evaluation rigor ka sahi level chun sakte hain. Aur jab aap failing application dekhte hain, to ye poochhna ek aadat bana lo ki failure kis gulf me aata hai: Comprehension — aapko abhi samajh nahi hai ki inputs kaise dikhte hain ya system un par kaise behave karta hai; pehle aur traces dekho, kuch change karne se pehle. Specification — aapki requirements LLM ke follow karne ke liye kaafi explicit nahi hain; prompt ya agent logic revise karo taaki gap close ho. Generalization — requirements clear hain, lekin LLM kuch inputs par phir bhi fail karta hai; measure karo ki failure kitni baar hota hai, aur stronger interventions consider karo, jaise zyada examples, behtar retrieval, ya fine-tuning.

Yaad rakho: Comprehension = "data asal me kaisa hai?", Specification = "maine LLM ko clearly bataya kya?", Generalization = "clear instructions ke baad bhi LLM kyun fail karta hai?" — teeno alag problems hain, aur teeno ke fix alag hain. Galat gulf ko fix karne se failure kabhi solve nahi hoga.
SOURCESource: Evals for AI Engineers, O'Reilly, Chapter 1 — Introduction

02Chapter 2 · LLMs and Evaluation Basics

LLMs and Evaluation Basics

Chapter 1 me humne evaluation aur uska role introduce kiya. Evaluate karne se pehle, hume kuch chahiye jise evaluate kiya ja sake. Ye chapter ek pehli application banane aur uske moving parts ko samajhne ke baare me hai — ek single API call se lekar complex agent loops tak.

Is chapter me kya seekhenge

  • Ek simple LLM agent kaise banayein, ek single API call se shuru karke.
  • LLM agents ke components — single calls se lekar complex agent loops tak.
  • Initial prompts kaise likhein.
  • Evaluation ke do main modes jo poori book me use hote hain: absolute evaluation — judge karna ki ek configuration (jaise specific prompt, model, ya tool setup) ship karne ke liye kaafi correct hai ya nahi; aur comparative evaluation — multiple options compare karna (A/B tests, pairwise, ranking, leaderboards) taaki decide ho sake kaunsa behtar hai.

Chapter ke end tak aapke paas ek clear mental model hoga ki LLM agent kya cheezon se banta hai, aur aapke application ke liye kis tarah ki evaluation karni hai.

"Agent" ka matlab — broad definition

Chapter 1 me humne LLM agent ko broadly define kiya tha: woh input leta hai, language model ko ek ya zyada baar call karta hai, possibly tools invoke karta hai ya documents retrieve karta hai, aur output banata hai. "Agent" shabd kabhi autonomy ya multi-step reasoning imply karta hai, lekin hum use poore range ke liye use karte hain. Bina tools ke ek single LLM call ek agent hai (degenerate case). Conversation history maintain karne wala chatbot ek agent hai. Ek system jo task complete karne ke liye loop me paanch tools call karta hai, woh bhi ek agent hai. In examples me jo badalta hai woh hai components ki sankhya aur woh kaise wire kiye gaye hain. Components ko hum increasing complexity ke order me cover karenge. Har component nayi capabilities laata hai, aur har ek ke saath apne failure modes bhi aate hain jin par nazar rakhni hai.

Autonomy — kitni freedom deni hai?

Ek design choice sabhi components par apply hoti hai: agent ko kitni autonomy deni hai. Ek end par aap agent ko fixed sequence of steps par constrain kar sakte hain, bina kisi discretion ke. Dusre end par aap agent ko har turn par decide karne de sakte hain ki kya karna hai — kaunsa tool call karna hai aur kab rukna hai. Zyada autonomy agent ko zyada flexible banati hai, lekin evaluate karna bhi mushkil kar deti hai, kyunki possible behaviors ki space har decision ke saath badhti hai. Autonomy ka sahi level task aur errors ki cost par depend karta hai; ise jaldi decide karna achha hai, kyunki ye affect karta hai ki aapko kya evaluate karna hai.

Code examples — LiteLLM

Is chapter ke saare code examples LiteLLM use karte hain, ek popular Python library jo alag LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, aur dusre) ko ek consistent syntax ke saath call karne ke liye unified interface deti hai. Code examples me ek specific model version pin ki gayi hai (jaise gpt-4o-2024-08-06). Jab tak aap ye padhenge, naye versions available honge — model string ko apne provider ke current version se replace kar dein; API patterns wahi rehte hain. Chapter 9 discuss karta hai ki reproducibility ke liye model versions pin karna kyun matter karta hai.

Running example — email summarizer

Har component ko concrete banane ke liye, poore chapter me ek running example use hota hai: imagine karo aap apne organization ke liye ek simple email summarizer bana rahe hain. Woh incoming email leta hai aur ek chhota summary banata hai jisme sender ka naam aur unki key requests shamil hoti hain. Har component is example par layer hota jayega — pehle single call, phir conversation, phir retrieval, phir tools, aur aakhir me agent loop.

Evaluation setups — absolute vs comparative

Evaluation setups literature me aur practice me kai tarah ke describe kiye gaye hain. Hum un sab ko do high-level sawalon me bucket kar sakte hain: "Kya ye system ship karne ke liye kaafi achha hai?" aur "In options me se kaunsa behtar kaam karta hai?" Pehla sawaal absolute evaluation mangta hai — judge karna ki aapka system correctness ke kisi standard ko meet karta hai ya nahi. Dusra comparative evaluation mangta hai — decide karna ki kai alternatives me se kaunsa best perform karta hai.

Absolute evaluation wahi hai jahan zyadaatar teams shuru karti hain. Aapne ek system banaya hai (jaise email summarizer apne pehle draft prompt ke saath) aur aapko jaanna hai ki kya woh use karne ke liye kaafi achha hai. Iska matlab hai pehle define karna ki "kaafi achha" ka matlab kya hai, phir check karna ki aapke outputs us bar ko meet karte hain ya nahi. Literature me absolute evaluation ke metrics aksar inme se ek group me aate hain: reference-based evaluation — aap model ke output ko labeled data se compare karte hain, jise aksar ground truth kehte hain. Ground truth task ke hisaab se human-written summary, extracted field (jaise naam ya date), classification label, ya structured record ho sakta hai. Email summarizer ke liye aap emails ka dataset taiyar karenge jin ke human-written summaries hain, phir har model output ko exact match, reference ke saath overlap, ya semantic similarity ke liye score karenge. Ye approach appealing hai kyunki ye clear right-wrong comparisons deta hai. Lekin iski do problems hain: labeled data banana mehenga hai, aur kai tasks ke multiple valid outputs hote hain. Ek achha summary keh sakta hai "Reset password; confirm email on file," jabki ek equally valid summary keh sakta hai "Help me log in; verify my registered address." Sirf ek reference ke against score karna perfectly achhe outputs ko penalize karta hai. Hum reference-based methods sirf tab recommend karte hain jab genuinely ek hi correct answer ho, jaise verify karna ki ek field sahi extract hui ya nahi.

Reference-free evaluation me aap output ko un criteria ke against check karte hain jo aap define karte hain, bina gold answer ke. Email summarizer ke liye aap verify kar sakte hain ki output me Sender: field hai, exactly teen bullet points bante hain, aur previous threads se quoted text avoid kiya gaya hai. Aap ye bhi check kar sakte hain ki woh details invent to nahi karta jo email me explicitly mention nahi hain. Correctness usually aise criteria ka set hoti hai (format, completeness, factuality), bajaye ek sahi answer se match karne ke. Aap in checks ko rules se automate kar sakte hain ya ek aur model ko judge ke roop me use kar sakte hain. Zyadaatar teams apne specific application ke liye labeled datasets se shuru nahi karti, isliye reference-free evaluation ek practical option hai. Ye book primarily reference-free methods par focus karti hai. Ye keh kar bhi, reference data me invest karna significantly pay off karta hai jab aap kar sakte hain. Human-labeled "golden" outputs ka ek chhota set bhi (jaise 50 se 100 examples) aapko ground truth deta hai jin ke against automated judges validate kar sakein, known-good cases par regressions pakad sakein, aur time ke saath improvement measure kar sakein. Chapter 3 ki error analysis process naturally in labeled examples ko traces padhne aur annotate karne ke byproduct ke roop me produce karti hai. Aur jaise-jaise agents long-running, multi-step workloads (jaise tool chains, RAG pipelines, multi-session workflows) karte hain, reference-based evaluation aur important hoti jati hai, kyunki LLM judges aur dusre reference-free methods complex multi-step outputs ke saath struggle karte hain, aur labeled ground truth zyada deterministic aur reliable hota hai. Jaise-jaise aapka product mature hota hai, in systems ke liye labeled evaluation datasets curate karne me time spend karna worth ho sakta hai.

Comparative evaluation tab aati hai jab aapke paas kuch reasonably kaam karne wala hai aur aap alternatives compare karna chahte hain — jaise alag prompts, models, ya retrieval methods. Ab sawaal "kya ye kaafi correct hai?" nahi hai, balki "in me se kaunsa behtar hai?" hai. Comparative evaluation typically in forms me hoti hai: pairwise comparison — har input ke liye aap do outputs generate karte hain, ek prompt A se aur ek prompt B se. Ek evaluator (human ya model) choose karta hai ki kaunsa output kisi criterion ko behtar meet karta hai. Email summarizer ke liye sawaal ho sakta hai: "Kaunsa output sender ki requests ko extra details add kiye bina zyada accurately capture karta hai?" Ranking aur leaderboards — sirf do outputs compare karne ke bajaye, evaluators same input ke liye teen ya zyada options rank karte hain. Kai inputs par in rankings ko aggregate karke system-level scores milte hain jo leaderboard ke roop me display hote hain. Public benchmarks jaise LMArena is format ko use karte hain alag AI models compare karne ke liye. Kuch companies internal leaderboards maintain karti hain taaki track kar sakein ki kaunsa prompt, model, ya configuration best perform karta hai.

Ye book comparative evaluation ko depth me cover nahi karti, kyunki zyadaatar teams ka pehla bottleneck ek single configuration ko reliably kaam karwana hota hai. Comparative evaluation tab useful hoti hai jab aapke paas working system ho aur aap alternatives me se chunna chahte hon (jaise do prompts, do models, ya do retrieval strategies). Us point par pairwise comparison early development decisions jaldi lene ka low-cost tareeka hai. Production changes ke liye jin ka measurable user impact ho, statistically rigorous A/B testing zyada appropriate hai. Chapter 9 touch karta hai ki comparative evaluation CI/CD workflow me kaise fit hoti hai.

Yaad rakho: Pehle absolute evaluation — "kya ye ship karne layak hai?" — phir comparative — "in me se kaunsa behtar hai?" Ulta order me kaam karna matlab hai do toote hue options me se behtar toota hua chunna.
SOURCESource: Evals for AI Engineers, O'Reilly, Chapter 2 — LLMs and Evaluation Basics

02.1Chapter 2 · LLMs and Evaluation Basics

LLM APIs aur Agents ke Components

LLM se programmatically interact karna samajhna agent banane ka pehla step hai. LLM APIs input ko message objects ki list ke roop me expect karti hain, jahan har message ke do fields hote hain: role aur content. Role field batata hai ki kaun bol raha hai, aur iski chaar values ho sakti hain.

Message roles — chaar roles

  • system: assistant ke liye overall behavior aur context set karta hai (jaise "You are a helpful assistant that summarizes emails"). Ye optional hai lekin har request me consistent behavior establish karne me madad karta hai.
  • user: human ya application se input represent karta hai jo request kar raha hai. Yahan aap actual task ya query dete hain.
  • assistant: LLM ke previous responses represent karta hai. Aap inhe include karte hain jab multiple turns me conversation history maintain karni ho.
  • tool: tool invocation ke results ko wapas LLM tak pahunchane ke liye use hota hai. 2026 tak har major provider ki API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Cohere, aur dusre) tool role support karti hai.

Ek single request ke liye aap typically ek ya do messages ki list bhejte hain: context set karne ke liye ek optional system message, aur aapki query ke saath ek user message. Multi-turn conversations ke liye aap har exchange ko alternating user aur assistant messages ke roop me list me append karte hain. Conversation issues debug karte waqt check karo ki user aur assistant messages sahi tareeke se alternate kar rahe hain. Mismatched roles errors ka common source hain.

Single LLM call — sabse simple agent

Sabse simple case ek single call hai model ko. Aap input prompt dete hain, model response generate karta hai, aur woh response user ko ya system ke agle stage ko pass ho jata hai. Koi tools nahi, koi retrieval nahi, koi memory nahi, koi loops nahi. Sirf ek prompt in, ek response out. Email summarizer ke liye ye ek prompt ho sakta hai jo email ki body lekar model se sender ka naam extract karne aur requests summarize karne ko kehta hai. LiteLLM me ye call kuch aisi dikhti hai: completion(model="gpt-4o-2024-08-06", messages=[system message "You are an assistant that summarizes emails.", user message "Extract the sender's name and summarize the key requests..." + email_text]) — aur response se response["choices"][0]["message"]["content"] nikaal kar print karte hain. Example output: "Sender: [Name]. Key requests: Reset her account password; Verify email on file."

Ek baat dhyaan me rakhni hai: default temperature setting (usually 0 se upar) ke saath LLM outputs nondeterministic hote hain. Wahi input har run par alag outputs de sakta hai. Evaluate karte waqt ya to reproducibility ke liye temperature=0 set karo, ya multiple samples chalakar confidence intervals report karo. Chapter 5 isko detail me cover karta hai. Aise single LLM calls applications banane ka natural starting point hain. Lekin modern applications aksar additional components combine karti hain — jaise related messages laane ke liye retrieval, internal systems query karne ke liye tools, ya multiple steps coordinate karne ke liye agent loops. Har component nayi capabilities laata hai, lekin apne potential failure modes bhi introduce karta hai.

Conversations — multi-turn interaction

Kai applications ek single request-response exchange par nahi rukti. Woh user aur model ko multiple turns me interact karne deti hain. Ye conversational setting wohi hai jise zyadaatar log chatbots, customer support assistants ya copilots se associate karte hain. Email example me, sirf ek user message par summary dene ke bajaye, system follow-up questions support kar sakta hai: User: "Summarize the email." Assistant: "Sender: [Name]. Key requests: reset her account password; verify email on file." User: "Does she mention her preferred contact method?" Assistant: "Yes. She asks to be contacted by phone."

Technically, ek conversation sirf LLM calls ki series hai jahan prompt me poori dialogue history (ya kam se kam recent turns) shamil hoti hai. Minimal illustration me aap messages list banate hain, pehli completion call karte hain, phir model ke reply ko assistant message ke roop me append karte hain, phir agla user message append karke dusri completion call karte hain. Conversation system ko natural interaction ke kareeb le aati hai. Lekin ye naye design choices bhi introduce karti hai: kitni dialogue history rakhni hai, context length kaise manage karni hai, aur turns me consistency kaise ensure karni hai. Ye saare aspects evaluation discuss karte waqt wapas aayenge.

Retrieval — RAG

Kabhi-kabhi LLM ko background knowledge chahiye hoti hai jo immediate input me nahi hoti. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ek common pattern hai: system knowledge base ya document store search karta hai, relevant passages pull karta hai, aur phir query aur retrieved context dono model ko deta hai. Email summarizer me retrieval same sender se prior messages ya related support tickets la sakta hai. Is tarah model naye message ko past correspondence ke light me samajh sakta hai — example ke liye, ye pehchan sakta hai ki "I still can't log in" ek ongoing password reset issue ko refer karta hai.

Retrieval ke do common approaches hain. Keyword-based methods documents ko is basis par rank karte hain ki query ke saath kitne words share karte hain. Standard algorithm hai BM25, information retrieval ka ek classic keyword-matching method jo 1990s se hai aur abhi bhi achha kaam karta hai. Keyword methods fast hote hain aur effective hote hain jab terminology stable ho, lekin woh kuch bhi miss kar dete hain jo query se alag tareeke se phrase kiya gaya ho. Embedding-based methods text ke har piece (query aur har document) ko numbers ki list me badal dete hain, jise embedding kehte hain, jahan similar meanings similar lists of numbers par map hote hain. Ranking phir numbers compare karke hoti hai, jo system ko meaning match karne deti hai chahe wording alag ho (jaise "reset my login" versus "can't sign in").

Ek typical retrieval flow ke do steps hote hain: (1) relevant items search karo, phir (2) un items ko LLM prompt me insert karo. Embedding wale example me past support emails ka ek chhota archive liya jata hai, embedding(model="text-embedding-3-small", ...) se embeddings banaye jate hain, aur cosine similarity se scores nikale jate hain — cosine similarity do embedding vectors ko -1 (opposite) se 1 (identical) tak score karti hai; zyada score ka matlab hai text meaning me kareeb hain. Sabse zyada score wala past email retrieve karke naye email ke saath prompt me combine kiya jata hai, aur model context-aware summary deta hai — jaise "Context: this continues a previous unresolved login issue." Keyword-based retrieval ko yahan swap kiya ja sakta hai, whoosh ya elasticsearch jaisi library use karke top BM25 match return karke. Aap jo bhi method chunein, retrieval system ke behavior ko badal deta hai: output ki quality ab is par depend karti hai ki kya retrieve hua aur model ne use kaise use kiya. Ye issues Chapter 7 me RAG evaluation discuss karte waqt wapas aate hain.

Tools — model se precise kaam karvana

Kuch tasks software se behtar handle hote hain, model se nahi. Exact math karna, system of record se information pull karna, ya date ya phone number jaise cheez ko reformat karna — in cases me model ko result khud produce karne ki koshish karne ke bajaye use tool call karne dena aasan aur zyada reliable hai. Tool ek function hai jise model call kar sakta hai. Practically, tools kisi bhi language me implement kiye ja sakte hain ya API endpoints ke roop me; yahan Python use hota hai kyunki code examples Python me hain. Hum function ko model ko describe karte hain, uske expected arguments ke saath, taaki model ko pata ho use kaise invoke karna hai. Jab model tool call karta hai, to hamara runtime function execute karta hai aur result ko wapas conversation me feed karta hai.

Email summarizer me, maan lo sender ne callback number diya hai jaise "Call me at (415) 555-9021 ext. 7". Agar aap use CRM me store karna chahte hain ya automated dialer me pass karna chahte hain, to aapko number standard format me chahiye hoga. Model par bharosa karne ke bajaye ki woh phone numbers ko consistently rewrite karega, aap use ek normalize_phone tool de sakte hain jo hamesha wahi output format deta hai. Tool ko model ko JSON schema ke saath describe kiya jata hai — naam normalize_phone, description "Convert a phone number to standardized E.164 format", aur parameters me number string. Code me flow ye hai: completion call karo tools=tools ke saath; agar response message me tool_calls hain, to pehle assistant ka message append karo, phir har call ke liye function execute karo (jaise phonenumbers library se E.164 format), result ko role: "tool" message ke roop me append karo, aur phir dobara completion call karo taaki model final summary bana sake — jaise "Preferred contact: +14155559021".

Ye approach chhoti utilities tak limited nahi hai. Practically, applications aksar calculators, calendar lookups, search engines ya CRM APIs jaise tools expose karti hain. Ye model ko task ke un parts handle karne dete hain jin me precision, data access ya existing systems ke saath integration chahiye. Lekin ek warning yaad rakhni hai: tools LLMs ko actions lene ki ability dete hain. Hamesha tool inputs validate karo aur security implications consider karo, usse pehle ki LLM ko aise functions call karne do jo data ya external systems modify karte hain. Retrieval ko bhi ek tool ke roop me dekha ja sakta hai: phone number return karne ke bajaye, function query ke basis par documents ka set return karta hai. Hum use yahan alag treat karte hain kyunki retrieval itna common building block hai.

Yaad rakho: Single call → conversation → retrieval → tools — har layer capability badhata hai, aur har layer apne failure modes bhi laata hai. Prototype single call se shuru karo, phir ek-ek karke components add karo, taaki har layer ko alag se evaluate kar sakein.
Single LLM call (litellm) — Book me chhapa code (Chapter 2)
from litellm import completion

response = completion(
    model="gpt-4o-2024-08-06",
    messages=[
         {
            "role": "system",
            "content": "You are an assistant that summarizes
emails."
         },
         {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Extract the sender's name and summarize "
                      "the key requests:\n\n" + email_text
         }
    ]
)

print(response["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
# Example output:
# "Sender: [Name]
# Key requests:
# - Reset her account password
# - Verify email on file"
Multi-turn conversation (litellm) — Book me chhapa code (Chapter 2)
from litellm import completion

messages = [
    {
        "role": "system",
        "content": ("You are an assistant that summarizes and "
                    "answers questions about emails.")
    },
    {"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this email:\n\n" +
email_text}
]

response1 = completion(model="gpt-4o-2024-08-06",
messages=messages)
print(response1["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
# "Sender: [Name]. Key requests: reset her account
password;
# verify email on file."

# Add the model's reply to the conversation and continue
messages.append({
    "role": "assistant",
    "content": response1["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
})
messages.append({
    "role": "user",
    "content": "Does she mention her preferred contact method?"
})

response2 = completion(model="gpt-4o-2024-08-06",
messages=messages)
print(response2["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
# "Yes. She asks to be contacted by phone."
Embedding-based retrieval + RAG-style prompt — Book me chhapa code (Chapter 2)
# Small archive of past support emails
past_emails = [
    "Ticket #4521: Please reset my password. I cannot log in.",
    "Ticket #4605: Could you verify my email address on file?",
    "Ticket #4710: I need help updating my phone number."
]

# Embedding-based retrieval
from litellm import embedding, completion
import numpy as np

# Cosine similarity scores two embedding vectors from -1
(opposite)
# to 1 (identical). Higher means the two pieces of text are
closer
# in meaning.
def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

corpus_response = embedding(
    model="text-embedding-3-small",
    input=past_emails
)
corpus_embeddings = [item["embedding"] for item in
corpus_response["data"]]

query_response = embedding(
    model="text-embedding-3-small",
    input=email_text
)
query_embedding = query_response["data"][0]["embedding"]
scores = [cosine_similarity(query_embedding, e) for e in
corpus_embeddings]
retrieved = past_emails[int(np.argmax(scores))]

# Combine retrieved context with the new email
messages = [
    {
        "role": "system",
        "content": "You are an assistant that summarizes emails
with "
                    "context."
    },
    {
         "role": "user",
         "content": (f"Email:\n{email_text}\n\n"
                     f"Related past email:\n{retrieved}")
    }
]

response = completion(model="gpt-4o-2024-08-06",
messages=messages)
print(response["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
# Example output:
# "Sender: [Name].
# Key requests: reset her account password and confirm contact
information.
# Context: this continues a previous unresolved login issue."
BM25 keyword retrieval (rank_bm25) — Book me chhapa code (Chapter 2)
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi
import numpy as np

# Small archive of past emails
past_emails = [
    "Ticket #4521: Please reset my password. I cannot log in.",
    "Ticket #4605: Could you verify my email address on file?",
    "Ticket #4710: I need help updating my phone number."
]

# Build BM25 index
tokenized_corpus = [doc.lower().split() for doc in past_emails]
bm25 = BM25Okapi(tokenized_corpus)

query = "I still can't log in."
tokenized_query = query.lower().split()

# Score and select the best match
scores = bm25.get_scores(tokenized_query)
best_doc = past_emails[int(np.argmax(scores))]

print(best_doc)
# Example output:
# "Ticket #4521: Please reset my password. I cannot log in."

02.2Chapter 2 · LLMs and Evaluation Basics

Agent Loops, Tools aur MCP

Ab tak humne single calls, conversations, retrieval aur tools ko alag-alag components ke roop me dekha hai. Ye sab broad sense me agents hain, lekin relatively simple hain. Sabse complex pattern hai agent loop. Is pattern me LLM current state receive karta hai, decide karta hai ki kya action lena hai, use execute karta hai, result observe karta hai, aur task complete hone tak repeat karta hai. Defining feature ye hai ki model har step khud decide karta hai, bajaye ek predetermined sequence follow karne ke.

Agent loop kaise kaam karta hai

Email summarizer example me, ek agent loop naye message ko padh kar shuru ho sakta hai aur decide kar sakta hai ki aur context chahiye. Woh same sender se past correspondence retrieve karta hai, result dekhta hai, aur phir callback number normalize karne ke liye ek tool call karta hai. Sirf un steps ke baad woh decide karta hai ki ab uske paas final summary banane ke liye kaafi information hai. Minimal sketch me loop kuch aisa dikhta hai: messages list banao, phir for step in range(10) — steps ki sankhya par cap lagao — har iteration me completion call karo tools=tools ke saath; agar model tool call request karta hai, to use run karo aur result append karke continue karo; agar model final answer deta hai, to print karo aur break karo.

LangChain, LlamaIndex aur AutoGPT jaise frameworks is pattern ko additional features ke saath wrap karte hain, jaise memory, planning strategies aur error handling. Blog posts ya papers padhte waqt agents ke baare me jargon aur seemingly complex ideas se overwhelm hona aasan hai. Lekin idea simple hai: agent loop sirf repeated LLM calls hain jo step by step decide karte hain ki text generate karna hai, information retrieve karni hai, tool call karna hai, ya task complete hone par rukna hai. Yaad rakho humne "agent" ko broadly define kiya tha — ek single LLM call bhi include hoti hai; loop pattern agent ka sabse complex form hai.

Loops ko bound karna — zaroori safety

Agent loops theoretically indefinitely chal sakte hain agar bound na kiye jayein. Hamesha ek maximum step count include karo (jaise example me range(10)) aur production systems me timeouts implement karne par consider karo. Bina cap ke, ek agent tool calls ke cycle me phans sakta hai, ya har step par naya sub-task banata hua kabhi ruk hi na sake — aur har step ki cost bhi hoti hai.

Multi-agent architectures

Is chapter ke examples me ek single agent assume kiya gaya hai, lekin kuch applications multiple agents use karti hain jo ek dusre ke saath coordinate karte hain. Multi-agent architectures additional evaluation challenges introduce karte hain, jaise kya agents sahi information ek dusre tak pass karte hain aur kya overall system coherent results deta hai. Is book ke evaluation principles phir bhi apply hote hain; main difference ye hai ki aapko individual agents aur unke interactions dono evaluate karne hote hain.

Model Context Protocol (MCP)

Tools ko aasan banane ki ek recent koshish hai Model Context Protocol (MCP). MCP ek standard tareeka define karta hai jisse ek tool server available functions describe kar sakta hai (unke naam, arguments aur authentication requirements samet) aur ek client unhe discover aur call kar sakta hai. Har service ke liye custom glue code likhne ke bajaye, aap apne application ko ek MCP server ki taraf point kar sakte hain aur model ke paas turant tools ka catalog aa jata hai jo woh use kar sakta hai.

MCP evaluation challenges bhi introduce karta hai jo hardcoded tool definitions ke saath nahi aate. Tool servers calls ke beech apne schemas add, remove ya change kar sakte hain, isliye ek agent jo kal kaam kar raha tha, aaj toot sakta hai kyunki ek tool signature badal gaya. Permission scoping bhi important ho jati hai: agar ek MCP server 50 tools expose karta hai lekin aapka agent sirf 3 use karna chahiye, to aapko verify karna hoga ki agent apne authorized set ke andar rehta hai. Hum Chapter 8 me tool use evaluate karne ke liye wapas aayenge.

Putting it together — loop ka mental model

Agent loop ko samajhne ka sabse simple tareeka hai ise ek cycle ke roop me dekhna: model current state par reason karta hai, decide karta hai ki act karna hai ya nahi (tool call karke ya context retrieve karke), result observe karta hai, aur final answer banane tak continue karta hai. Yehi cycle ReAct pattern (Reason + Act) ke peeche hai, jo prompting wale section me detail me aata hai. Har iteration me model ke paas teen choices hoti hain — text generate karo, action lo, ya ruko. Evaluation ke liye iska matlab hai ki aapko sirf final output nahi, poori trace evaluate karni hai: model ne kaunse steps liye, kaunse tools kab call kiye, aur kahan usne galat turn liya.

Yaad rakho: Agent loop = decide → act → observe → repeat, hamesha step cap ke saath. MCP tools ko plug-and-play banata hai, lekin schema drift aur permission scoping uski apni evaluation challenges laate hain.
Tool calling — normalize_phone (litellm) — Book me chhapa code (Chapter 2)
from litellm import completion
import json
import phonenumbers

# Define the tool as a Python function
def normalize_phone(number: str):
    parsed = phonenumbers.parse(number, "US")
    return phonenumbers.format_number(
        parsed, phonenumbers.PhoneNumberFormat.E164
    )

# Tell the model what the tool is and how to call it
tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "normalize_phone",
            "description": "Convert a phone number to "
                           "standardized E.164 format",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {"number": {"type": "string"}},
                "required": ["number"]
            }
        }
    }
]

messages = [
    {
        "role": "system",
        "content": "You summarize emails and may call tools when
helpful."
    },
    {"role": "user", "content": f"Summarize this
email:\n\n{email_text}"}
]

resp = completion(model="gpt-4o-2024-08-06", messages=messages,
tools=tools)
msg = resp["choices"][0]["message"]

# If the model calls the tool, run it and send back the result
if "tool_calls" in msg:
    # First, append the assistant's own message (which carries
the tool_calls)
    messages.append(msg)
    for call in msg["tool_calls"]:
        if call["function"]["name"] == "normalize_phone":
            args = json.loads(call["function"]["arguments"])
            result = normalize_phone(**args)
            messages.append({
                "role": "tool",
                "tool_call_id": call["id"],
                "name": "normalize_phone",
                "content": json.dumps(result)
            })

# Continue the conversation until the model produces a final
summary
resp2 = completion(model="gpt-4o-2024-08-06", messages=messages,
tools=tools)
print(resp2["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
# Example:
# "Sender: [Name]. Key requests: reset her account
password.
# Preferred contact: +14155559021"
Minimal agent loop sketch — Book me chhapa code (Chapter 2)
# Minimal sketch of an agent loop
from litellm import completion

messages = [
    {
        "role": "system",
        "content": ("You are an agent that can retrieve past
emails, "
                    "call tools, and summarize.")
    },
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": f"Summarize this new email:\n\n{email_text}"
    }
]

for step in range(10): # cap the number of steps
    resp = completion(model="gpt-4o-2024-08-06",
messages=messages, tools=tools)
    msg = resp["choices"][0]["message"]

    # If the model requests a tool, run it and append the result
    if "tool_calls" in msg:
        messages.append(msg) # append the assistant turn with
tool_calls
        # (execute retrieval or tool functions here)
        messages.append({
            "role": "tool",
            "tool_call_id": msg["tool_calls"][0]["id"],
            "content": "Tool result goes here"
        })
        continue
    # If the model produces a final answer, stop
    if msg.get("content"):
        print("Final output:", msg["content"])
        break
Tool spec JSON (OpenAPI-style) — Book me chhapa code (Chapter 2)
{
  "type": "function",
  "function": {
    "name": "normalize_phone",
    "description": "Convert a phone number to standardized E.164
format",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "number": {
          "type": "string",
          "description": "Phone number to normalize, assumed to
be US "
                         "if no country code is provided"
        }
      },
      "required": ["number"]
    }
  }
}

02.3Chapter 2 · LLMs and Evaluation Basics

Fundamentals of Prompting

Ab tak humne LLM agent ke architectural components cover kiye hain — single calls, conversations, retrieval, tools aur agent loop. Ek aur set of fundamentals hai ki un components ko drive karne wale prompts kaise likhein. Ek achha prompt itna specific hota hai ki model ko guide kare, aur itna consistent hota hai ki predictable outputs de. Time ke saath aap use refine karenge, lekin ek strong starting point me kuch recurring pieces hote hain.

Ek achhe prompt ke pieces

Ek achhe first-draft prompt me usually ye elements hote hain:

  • Role: Model ko batao ki woh kaun hai. Ye use sahi domain me anchored rakhta hai.
  • Objective: Clearly batao ki task kya hai aur success kaisa dikhta hai.
  • Instructions: Dos aur don'ts spell out karo. Example: agar teen bullet points chahiye to wahi kaho. Agar quoted text exclude karna hai to explicit banao.
  • Context: Woh data do jis par model ko act karna hai, jaise email, document, ya koi aur text snippets. Context ke bina woh sirf guess kar sakta hai.
  • Reasoning: Mushkil tasks ke liye aap model se keh sakte hain ki answer return karne se pehle apni reasoning explain kare. Older models ko explicit "think step by step" instructions se fayda hota hai; naye reasoning models (jaise OpenAI ki o-series ya DeepSeek R1) internal chains of thought automatically generate karte hain, isliye in instructions ko add karna actually performance hurt kar sakta hai, kyunki ye model ki apni reasoning process me interfere karta hai.
  • Output format: Describe karo ki answer kaise structure hona chahiye, taaki use downstream aasani se consume kiya ja sake.
  • Examples: Optional lekin powerful. Ek chhota input-output pair format, style aur detail ka level dikhata hai.
  • Delimiters: Section headers, code fences ya tags use karo taaki instructions, context aur examples alag rahein.

Prompt templates

Practically, aap typically in elements ko ek prompt template me organize karte hain — ek reusable structure jis me variable content ke liye placeholders hote hain jo runtime par fill hote hain. Example ke liye, [PASTE EMAIL TEXT HERE] placeholder ko actual email text se replace kar diya jayega jab application chalegi. Templates use karne se prompts maintain, debug aur version control karne me aasan hote hain, kyunki aap poora prompt dobara likhe bina specific sections modify kar sakte hain.

Ek email summarizer ka prompt template kuch aisa dikhta hai: Role — "You are an assistant for our internal support team." Objective — "Extract the sender's name and summarize the key requests in an incoming email." Instructions — up to teen concise bullet points; quoted text from prior threads ya signatures include mat karo; tone plain aur professional rakho. Context — [PASTE EMAIL TEXT HERE]. Reasoning — sender aur requests extract karne ke liye needed steps socho, lekin sirf final formatted output return karo. Output format — "Sender:" phir "Requests:" ke neeche bullets. Example — Input: "My account was locked after travel. Please reset it and call me at (415) 555-9021. – [Name]" → Output: Sender: [Name]; Requests: Reset account access; Call back at (415) 555-9021.

Template ka ek aur fayda hai ki ye prompts refine karna aasan bana deta hai. Maan lo aap discover karte hain ki model kabhi summaries me quoted email threads include kar leta hai, aur aap nahi chahte ki summaries me previous emails ki zyada information aaye. Structured template ke saath aapko exactly pata hai kahan fix karna hai. Instructions section me ek line add karo: "Do not include quoted text from prior threads." Ya imagine karo aapko realize hota hai ki summaries me support agent ke liye clear call to action hamesha nahi hota. Aap format section me ek naya field add kar sakte hain, jaise "Next action for agent:". Overall, ek lambe block me ad hoc notes pile karne ke bajaye, template changes ko organized aur maintain karne me aasan rakhta hai.

Tip: Apne prompt templates ko hardcode karne ke bajaye alag files ya configuration ke roop me store karo. Unhe version control me commit karo, aur har version ko tag ya hash karo taaki aap kisi bhi output ko exactly us prompt tak trace kar sakein jisne use banaya tha. Traces log karte waqt prompt version ko model version aur input ke saath record karo; isse ye batana possible hota hai ki behavior change prompt edit se aaya, model update se, ya data shift se.

Retrieval fundamentals — keyword se shuru karo

Jab aap apne application me retrieval implement karte hain, to hum recommend karte hain ki keyword search se shuru karo. Ye set up karne me fast hai, interpret karne me aasan hai, aur aksar ek bahut strong baseline hota hai. BM25 jaise keyword methods ke saath aap exactly dekh sakte hain ki ek document kyun retrieve hua, kyunki query terms uske saath overlap karte hain. Ye transparency debugging ko straightforward banati hai, aur kai domains me stable vocabulary (jaise support tickets) ke saath keyword search surprisingly achha perform karta hai.

Ek toy example rank_bm25 library use karta hai past support emails ki chhoti list par: corpus ko tokenize karo (doc.lower().split()), BM25Okapi(tokenized_corpus) banao, query "I still can't log in." ko tokenize karo, bm25.get_scores(tokenized_query) se scores nikalo aur best match chuno — is case me "Ticket #4521: Please reset my password. I cannot log in." Ye sirf ek toy demonstration hai. Practically, aapka corpus thousands of emails ya tickets ho sakta hai jo database me store hain, aur aap database ki apni retrieval features ya ek dedicated search library use karenge indexing aur ranking handle karne ke liye. Important baat ye hai ki aap ek simple, interpretable baseline se shuru karein. Wahan se, agar aap paate hain ki woh relevant cases miss karta hai, to aap embedding search par ja sakte hain, ya hybrid search par — jo keyword aur dense retrieval scores ko reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) jaisi method se combine karta hai. Hybrid search kai production RAG systems me default ban gaya hai kyunki keyword matching exact terms pakadta hai jo embeddings miss karte hain, jabki embeddings semantic similarity pakadte hain jo keywords miss karte hain. Zyadaatar vector databases (jaise Pinecone, Weaviate aur Qdrant) hybrid search natively support karte hain.

Tools aur agents — ReAct pattern

Jab aap pehli baar ek application me tools add karte hain, to main step hai unhe model ko clearly describe karna. Zyadaatar modern APIs OpenAPI ki style me specification expect karti hain: ek function naam, ek chhoti description, aur uske arguments ke liye JSON schema. Precision matter karta hai. Aisi descriptions likho jo exactly explain karein ki function kya karta hai, arguments ko unambiguously define karein, aur edge cases ke baare me sochein. Example: agar ek number string hona chahiye to wahi kaho. Agar tool sirf US phone numbers ke liye kaam karta hai to explicit banao. Specification jitni clear hogi, model ke tool use karte waqt mistakes karne ki gunjaish utni kam hogi. normalize_phone ke liye tool spec me description hoti hai "Convert a phone number to standardized E.164 format", parameters me number string, aur description me ye bhi ki agar country code na diya jaye to US assume kiya jata hai.

Ek first-pass tool prompt wahi template reuse kar sakta hai jo humne pehle develop kiya tha (role, objective, context, instructions, format). Ek hi addition hai — ek section jo available tools list karta hai aur explain karta hai ki unhe kab use karna chahiye. Example: "You summarize emails. You may call normalize_phone whenever a phone number is present. Always include the tool's result in the final summary." Tool spec ke saath combine karke, ye ek simple tool-enabled agent chalane ke liye kaafi hai.

Jab prompts, retrieval aur tools jagah par aa jayein, to aap unhe ek agent me combine kar sakte hain. Agent simply ek system hai jo is cycle se loop karta hai: model current state ke baare me reason karta hai, decide karta hai ki act karna hai ya nahi (tool call karke ya context retrieve karke), result observe karta hai, aur final answer banane tak continue karta hai. Is pattern ko aksar ReAct (Reason + Act) kehte hain. Modern LLM APIs ab ReAct loop ka zyada hissa internally handle karti hain; tool calling APIs automatically reasoning aur action ko interleave kar deti hain, bina explicit ReAct prompts ke. Pattern phir bhi samajhna useful hai, kyunki underlying structure wahi hai.

Ek ReAct-style agent prompt email summarizer ke liye kuch aisa dikhta hai: Role — agent jo support emails summarize karne me madad karta hai. Objective — naya email padho, jab helpful ho retrieval aur tools use karo, aur support team ke liye final summary banao. Instructions — agar zaroorat ho to past tickets retrieve kar sakte ho; phone number ho to normalize_phone call kar sakte ho; step by step kaam karo, har step par ek action decide karo (retrieve, tool call, ya final answer ke saath ruko); action ke baad tumhe Observation milega, use agla step decide karne ke liye use karo; specified format me final answer ke saath end karo. Reasoning (ReAct pattern) — Thought → Action → Observation cycle follow karo: Thought — kya karne ka irada hai, uska brief statement; Action — JSON arguments ke saath call karne wala tool; Observation — har action ke baad provide kiya jayega; final answer banane tak repeat karo. Ek step format example me Thought hota hai "I should check prior tickets for context", Action retrieve_tickets with Args {"query": "can't log in; password reset"}, Observation ticket #4521, phir Thought "A phone number is present; I will normalize it", Action normalize_phone with Args {"number": "(415) 555-9021 ext. 7"}, Observation "+14155559021", aur phir final answer: Sender, Requests aur Phone ke saath.

Ambiguity par agent ko kitni freedom deni hai

Agent banane me ek important design choice hai use kitni freedom deni hai. Example: agar aap chahte hain ki woh cautious rahe aur user ki taraf se guess karne se bache, to instruction include karo: "If anything is ambiguous, always ask the user to clarify before proceeding." Agar aap chahte hain ki woh zyada autonomous ho, to iske bajaye kaho: "If anything is ambiguous, infer the most likely intent and continue." Is decision ko prompt me explicit banana agent ko zyada predictable aur baad me evaluate karne me aasan bana deta hai.

Prototype se evaluation tak

Ab aapke paas LLM agent ke building blocks hain: single LLM calls, conversations, retrieval, tools aur agent loops. Aap do main evaluation approaches samajh gaye hain: absolute evaluation (kya ye kaafi achha hai?) aur comparative evaluation (kaunsa behtar hai?). Aapne prompts ko templates se structure karna seekh liya hai. Jab aap apna prototype real data par chalayeinge, to aapko problems milengi. Model instructions ko alag inputs par alag tareeke se interpret kar sakta hai. Retrieval irrelevant documents return kar sakta hai. Output quality unpredictably vary kar sakti hai. Ye problems aapki evaluation ka starting point hain. Agla chapter dikhata hai ki in problems ko systematically analyze kaise karein — representative examples kaise collect karein, alag tarah ke failures categorize kaise karein, aur do root causes me farq kaise karein: specification failures (jahan aapka prompt unclear ya incomplete tha) aur generalization failures (jahan model clear instructions ke bawjood inconsistently behave karta hai). Ye systematic error analysis hi poori book me aage aane wali har cheez ki foundation hai.

Yaad rakho: Prompt ek template hai, ek block nahi — role, objective, instructions, context, reasoning, format, examples. Jab kuch galat ho, to template batata hai ki fix kahan karna hai. Aur ambiguity par agent ka behavior prompt me decide karo, baad me guess mat karo.
Example 2-1 — Prompt template for email summarizer — Book me chhapa code (Chapter 2)
### Role
You are an assistant for our internal support team.

### Objective
Extract the sender's name and summarize the key requests in an
incoming email.

### Instructions
- Produce up to three concise bullet points for the requests.
- Do not include quoted text from prior threads or signatures.
- Keep the tone plain and professional.

### Context
[PASTE EMAIL TEXT HERE]

### Reasoning
Think through the steps needed to extract the sender and requests,
but return only the final formatted output.

### Output format
- Sender:
- Requests:
-
-
-

### Example
Input: "My account was locked after travel. Please reset it and
call me at (415) 555-9021. – [Name]"
Output:
- Sender: [Name]
- Requests:
- Reset account access
- Call back at (415) 555-9021
Example 2-2 — Agent prompt (ReAct-style) — Book me chhapa code (Chapter 2)
### Role
You are an agent that helps summarize support emails.

### Objective
Read a new email, use retrieval and tools when helpful, and produce
a final summary for the support team.

### Instructions
- You may retrieve past tickets if needed.
- You may call `normalize_phone` when a phone number is present.
- Work step by step. At each step, decide on one action
(retrieve, call a tool, or stop with a final answer).
- After you take an Action, you will receive an Observation,
with the result. Use it to decide your next step.
- End with a final answer in the specified format.
- If the user's request is ambiguous, [choose one]:
**(a)** ask a clarifying question before proceeding;
**(b)** infer the most likely intent and continue.

### Reasoning (ReAct pattern)
Follow the Thought → Action → Observation cycle:
- **Thought:** (optional, for development) a brief statement of
what
you intend to do.
- **Action:** the tool to call, with JSON arguments.
- **Observation:** will be provided after each action.
- Repeat until you produce the final answer.

### Output format (for Final)
Final answer:
- Sender:
- Requests:
-
-
-
- Phone:

### Step format example
Thought: I should check prior tickets for context.
Action: retrieve_tickets
Args: {"query": "can't log in; password reset", "sender": ""}

Observation: [{"id":"4521","text":"Please reset my password. I
cannot log in."}]

Thought: A phone number is present; I will normalize it.
Action: normalize_phone
Args: {"number": "(415) 555-9021 ext. 7"}

Observation: "+14155559021"

Thought: I have enough information to write the summary.
Final answer:
- Sender: [Name]
- Requests:
- Reset account access
- Verify email on file
- Call back at
- Phone: +14155559021
SOURCESource: Evals for AI Engineers, O'Reilly, Chapter 2 — LLMs and Evaluation Basics
